contents.name: 5.1 The Standard Turing Machine Model
Definition 5.1.1 A standard Turing machine (TM)
The next-state function gives one action for each state and scanned tape symbol
The single-ended tape, left-adjusted input, and blank convention of §5.1
The TM accepts the language L(M), and a language is decidable when some TM halts on every input and accepts exactly the strings in it
A TM M computes a function f : Γ* ↦→ Γ* ∪ {⊥}
5.2 Extensions to the Standard Turing Machine Model
5.2.1 Multi-Tape Turing Machines
Theorem 5.2.1 For each k-tape Turing machine Mk there is a one-tape Turing machine M1 such that a terminating T-step computation by Mk can be simulated in O(T^2) steps by M1
contents.reason: Page 597 only fixes the machine variants themselves. The actual simulation and overhead theorem is the opening core of `robust-machine-models-and-universal-computation`, where the equivalence of one-tape, multitape, and other machine models is proved.

contents.name: 5.2.2 Nondeterministic Turing Machines
Definition 5.2.1 A nondeterministic Turing machine (NDTM)
An NDTM accepts string w if there is some choice string c such that the last state entered by M is h
Theorem 5.2.2 Any language accepted by a nondeterministic standard TM can be accepted by a standard deterministic one
contents.reason: The present page introduces nondeterministic acceptance but does not yet prove equivalence with deterministic recognizability. The simulation theorem itself is one of the named A-page results on `robust-machine-models-and-universal-computation`.

contents.name: 5.3 Configuration Graphs
Definition 5.3.1 The configuration of a standard Turing machine M at any point in time
Definition 5.3.2 The configuration of a k-tape Turing machine M
contents.reason: This page only names multitape machines as a model variant. The full configuration calculus for multitape simulations becomes load-bearing one page later, where the one-tape simulation theorems and universal-machine coding are developed.

contents.name: Definition 5.3.3 A configuration graph G(MND, w) associated with the NDTM MND
Figure 5.9 The configuration graph G(MND, w) of a nondeterministic Turing machine on input w
The graph is acyclic because the source applies configuration graphs only to machines that halt on all inputs
contents.reason: Page 597 must also handle recognizers and nondeterministic branches that loop forever. For that reason the scaffold defines configuration graphs without importing Savage's extra halting-on-all-inputs acyclicity convention.

contents.name: TM Configurations
A configuration of a TM is a triple (state, head position, tape contents) representing a snapshot in time
Encoding a configuration as a string by inserting the state symbol at the head position
TM Computation Histories
An (accepting) computation history for TM M on input w is a sequence of configurations C1, C2, ..., Caccept that M enters until it accepts
Encode a computation history C1, C2, ..., Caccept as the string #C1##C2#...##Caccept
Theorem: ELBA is decidable
contents.reason: The decidability of LBA emptiness is a later automata-undecidability topic, not part of the foundational machine-semantics page. Here it is used only as background for why one can algorithmically test a finite computation history.

contents.name: Construct LBA A_{M,w} that checks whether its input begins with the right start configuration, each successive configuration legally follows, and the final configuration is accepting
Theorem: ELBA is undecidable
contents.reason: The undecidability reduction target belongs to the later language-undecidability pages. It is not part of the dependency-closed semantic scaffold needed before universal machines and the halting problem are developed.

contents.name: Theorem: PCP is undecidable
contents.reason: The computation-history reduction to Post correspondence is a later undecidability application. The current page only harvests the local history-checking mechanism that the reduction uses.

contents.name: Theorem: ALLCFG is undecidable
contents.reason: Universality for context-free grammars is not yet in scope on page 597. Sipser's proof matters here only because it spells out a PDA that checks invalid computation histories, and the actual undecidability statement belongs with the later language-undecidability page.
